description: Article-based learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway.

cards.title: Wrong Has Degrees
cards.subtitle: Flat Earth vs perfect sphere—both wrong, but one is MORE wrong.
body: The flat Earth theory is wrong by a lot. The spherical Earth theory is wrong by a tiny amount.
Progress isn't replacing wrong with right—it's replacing very wrong with slightly less wrong.
cards.takeaway: Scientific progress is measured in degrees of wrongness, not binary truth.

cards.title: Flat Earth Was Reasonable
cards.subtitle: Stand anywhere. Look around. It looks flat.
body: For most of history, flat Earth wasn't ignorance—it was observation.
The Greeks noticed ships disappearing hull-first. They calculated Earth's circumference within 10%.
cards.takeaway: Local observations can be misleading. Scale reveals what proximity hides.

cards.title: The Sphere Was an Improvement
cards.subtitle: Earth bulges at the equator and flattens at the poles.
body: Newton predicted Earth would be slightly squashed. The equatorial diameter is 27 miles longer than the polar.
On an 8,000-mile planet, that's only 0.3% deviation. Refined, not replaced.
cards.takeaway: Better measurements don't overthrow old theories—they refine them.

cards.title: Even the Oblate Spheroid Is Wrong
cards.subtitle: Earth is lumpy. Mountains, trenches, tectonic plates.
body:
• Everest sticks up 5 miles
• Mariana Trench drops 7 miles
• The geoid looks like a lumpy potato
Each refinement captures more detail. None captures everything.
cards.takeaway: Reality is always more complicated than our models. Models are still useful.

cards.title: Newton Wasn't Wrong—Just Incomplete
cards.subtitle: Einstein showed where Newton's equations stop being accurate.
body: Newtonian physics works perfectly for everyday speeds. We still use it to land rockets.
At very high speeds or strong gravity, Newton drifts from reality. Einstein accounts for the drift.
cards.takeaway: Superseded theories often remain useful within their domain of accuracy.

cards.title: Einstein Will Also Be Refined
cards.subtitle: General relativity breaks down inside black holes.
body: Einstein's equations predict singularities—points where the math stops working.
When someone combines quantum mechanics and gravity, Einstein becomes a special case.
cards.takeaway: Every theory eventually reveals its boundaries. That's how science advances.

cards.title: Refinement, Not Revolution
cards.subtitle: Copernicus didn't prove Ptolemy stupid—he provided a simpler model.
body: Ptolemy's geocentric model worked. The math was just ugly.
Copernicus noticed math got simpler with Sun at center. Kepler refined it with ellipses.
cards.takeaway: Scientific revolutions usually simplify rather than overthrow.

cards.title: Wrongness Is Asymptotic
cards.subtitle: We keep getting closer to truth without quite reaching it.
body: Each generation inherits slightly-less-wrong theories and makes them less wrong still.
The improvements get smaller as we get closer. Always toward accuracy, never arriving at perfection.
cards.takeaway: Science approaches truth asymptotically—ever closer, never complete.

cards.title: Context Determines Acceptable Wrong
cards.subtitle: Walking to the store? Flat Earth is fine. Launching satellites? You need the geoid.
body: A carpenter doesn't need relativity. A GPS satellite does.
The 'wrong' theory that's accurate enough for your purpose is effectively right.
cards.takeaway: Practical truth depends on the precision your application requires.

cards.title: Cynicism Misses the Point
cards.subtitle: 'Science is always changing' describes how knowledge improves.
body: The cynic says: scientists were wrong before. The answer: they're less wrong now.
The alternative to imperfect knowledge isn't perfect knowledge—it's ignorance.
cards.takeaway: Acknowledging uncertainty is a feature, not a bug.

cards.title: Error Bars Shrink Over Time
cards.subtitle: Light speed measurements: 27% off in 1676. Exact by definition now.
body: Each generation of instruments tightened the bounds. Values didn't jump randomly—they converged.
That convergence is the signature of getting less wrong.
cards.takeaway: Shrinking error bars prove theories are converging on something real.

cards.title: Being Wrong Is Required
cards.subtitle: If you're never wrong, you're not learning anything new.
body: Every useful theory started as a guess. The partially wrong ones got refined.
The goal isn't to be right—it's to become less wrong faster than everyone else.
cards.takeaway: Science progresses by being wrong in increasingly precise ways.
